questions.stem: Which compound is a secondary amine?
questions.explanation: Amines are classified by the number of carbon groups bonded to the nitrogen: CH₃NHCH₂CH₃ has two. CH₃CH(NH₂)CH₃ is still a primary amine because its nitrogen has only one carbon attached, even though that carbon is in the middle of the chain.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of CH₃CH(NH₂)CH₃?
questions.explanation: The NH₂ group is on carbon 2 of a three-carbon chain, so the name is propan-2-amine. Dimethylamine is (CH₃)₂NH, a secondary amine with the nitrogen between the two carbons.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of H₂NCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂NH₂?
questions.explanation: Six carbons with an amino group at each end give hexane-1,6-diamine, one of the monomers of nylon-6,6. An amide contains C=O bonded to N, which this molecule does not have.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂NH₂?
questions.explanation: The main chain has three carbons, numbered from the end bearing the NH₂ group, with a methyl branch on carbon 2. 2-methylbutan-1-amine would have five carbon atoms altogether.

questions.stem: Why can amines act as bases?
options: The N-H bond breaks easily, so the amine donates a proton
The nitrogen atom carries a positive charge in the neutral molecule
The lone pair on the nitrogen atom can accept a proton
The amino group releases hydroxide ions directly from the molecule
questions.explanation: A base is a proton acceptor, and the non-bonding pair on nitrogen forms a bond to H⁺. In water this produces OH⁻ from water molecules: RNH₂ + H₂O ⇌ RNH₃⁺ + OH⁻. Donating a proton would make the amine an acid.

questions.stem: What is the protonated form of ethanamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂?
questions.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair accepts H⁺, giving the ethylammonium ion with three hydrogens on nitrogen and a positive charge. CH₃CH₂NH⁻ is what would form if the amine lost a proton.

questions.stem: Which equation shows methanamine acting as a base in water?
questions.explanation: Methanamine accepts a proton from water, forming the methylammonium ion and hydroxide ions, so the solution is basic. Losing a proton to water would be acid behaviour.

questions.stem: Many drugs containing an amine group, such as lignocaine, are supplied as their hydrochloride salts for injection. Why?
options: The salt has stronger covalent bonds, so it does not react with any molecules in the body
The protonated amine is ionic, so it forms ion-dipole interactions and is more soluble in water
The hydrochloride salt is non-polar, so it passes more easily through the watery blood plasma
The chloride ion is the active part of the drug, so the salt is a more concentrated dose
questions.explanation: Protonating the amine gives a cation that, with its chloride counter-ion, is strongly hydrated by water. The neutral amine relies on weaker hydrogen bonding, and its hydrocarbon parts limit solubility.

questions.stem: Propan-1-amine boils at a higher temperature than its isomer trimethylamine, (CH₃)₃N, but lower than propan-1-ol. Which explanation is best?
options: Trimethylamine is ionic, and nitrogen is more electronegative than oxygen in a molecule
Trimethylamine has no N-H bonds, and N-H hydrogen bonds are weaker than O-H hydrogen bonds
Trimethylamine is more polar, and amines have stronger dispersion forces than alcohols
Propan-1-amine has more electrons, and O-H covalent bonds break when an alcohol boils
questions.explanation: A tertiary amine has no H on nitrogen, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. Primary amines can, but nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so their hydrogen bonds are weaker than those in alcohols.

questions.stem: An aqueous solution of butan-1-amine is shaken with dilute hydrochloric acid. What forms?
questions.explanation: An amine neutralises an acid by accepting a proton, forming an alkylammonium salt. This is an acid-base reaction; no carbon-nitrogen bond is broken.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of CH₃COOCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The CH₃CO part comes from ethanoic acid and the OCH₂CH₃ part from ethanol. The alkyl group from the alcohol is named first, then the acid part with the ending -oate.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of CH₃CH₂CH₂COOCH₃?
questions.explanation: The acid part, CH₃CH₂CH₂CO, has four carbons including the C=O carbon, so it is butanoate; the CH₃ on the single-bonded oxygen comes from methanol. Counting only three carbons gives methyl propanoate.

questions.stem: What is the systematic name of HCOOCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: HCO comes from methanoic acid, which has one carbon, and the ethyl group comes from ethanol. Methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃, is an isomer, but the carbon counts sit on opposite sides of the ester group.

questions.stem: Which carboxylic acid and alcohol react to form ethyl pentanoate?
questions.explanation: The alkyl group named first, ethyl, comes from the alcohol; the -oate part, pentanoate, comes from the acid. Ethanoic acid and pentan-1-ol give the isomer pentyl ethanoate.

questions.stem: What is the condensed formula of the ester formed from propanoic acid and methanol?
questions.explanation: The OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol's OH leave as water, joining CH₃CH₂CO- to -OCH₃. CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ is ethyl ethanoate, an isomer made from ethanoic acid and ethanol.

questions.stem: Why are esters usually prepared by heating under reflux?
options: Reflux removes the ester from the flask as soon as it forms, so the yield becomes 100%
Heating is needed to make the reaction exothermic, and the condenser removes the heat
Reflux lets oxygen from the air reach the mixture, which is needed to form the ester
Heating speeds up the slow reaction, and the condenser returns volatile vapours to the flask
questions.explanation: Condensation reactions are slow at 25 °C, so the mixture is heated. A vertical condenser cools the vapours of the volatile alcohol, acid and ester so they run back into the flask instead of escaping.

questions.stem: What is the role of a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid in the preparation of an ester?
options: It is the source of the oxygen atom in the ester
It neutralises the carboxylic acid before reaction
It oxidises the alcohol to the corresponding acid
It catalyses the reaction, increasing its rate
questions.explanation: Only a trace is added because the acid acts as a catalyst, providing a pathway of lower activation energy. It is not a reactant, and an oxidising agent such as dichromate would be needed to oxidise the alcohol.

questions.stem: Ethyl ethanoate and butanoic acid have the same molecular formula, C₄H₈O₂. Why does the ester boil at a much lower temperature?
options: Ester molecules have no O-H group, so they cannot hydrogen bond to each other
Ester molecules are non-polar, so only dispersion forces act between them
The ester has a smaller molar mass, so its dispersion forces are much weaker
The ester's covalent bonds are weaker, so less energy is needed to boil it
questions.explanation: Butanoic acid molecules hydrogen bond through their COOH groups. The ester group is polar, so dipole-dipole interactions act, but with no H on oxygen there is no hydrogen bonding between ester molecules. Both compounds have the same molar mass.

questions.stem: Methyl ethanoate is heated with dilute hydrochloric acid. What are the products?
questions.explanation: Acidic hydrolysis breaks the ester bond, reversing its formation and producing the parent carboxylic acid and alcohol. A carboxylate salt forms only in alkaline hydrolysis.

questions.stem: Ethyl propanoate is heated with sodium hydroxide solution. What are the products?
questions.explanation: In alkaline hydrolysis the acid produced reacts with hydroxide, so it is present as the carboxylate salt; the alcohol is released unchanged. The propanoate part comes from the acid side of the ester.

questions.stem: Use H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0. What mass of sodium hydroxide is needed to hydrolyse 3.70 g of methyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₃, completely?
questions.explanation: M(CH₃COOCH₃) = 74.0 g mol⁻¹, so n = 3.70 / 74.0 = 0.0500 mol. One OH⁻ reacts with each ester group, so n(NaOH) = 0.0500 mol and m = 0.0500 × 40.0 = 2.00 g.

questions.stem: Which pair of monomers can form a polyester?
questions.explanation: A polyester needs monomers with two reactive groups each, here two OH groups and two COOH groups, so that ester links can form at both ends. Ethanol and ethanoic acid each have one group and stop at a single ester; the diamine and diacid give a polyamide.

questions.stem: What is the repeating unit of the polyester formed from ethane-1,2-diol and hexanedioic acid?
questions.explanation: Each ester link joins a C=O carbon of the diacid to an oxygen of the diol, with water lost. Hexanedioic acid has six carbons, four of them CH₂, so the unit contains (CH₂)₄ between two C=O groups.

questions.stem: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH, polymerises to poly(lactic acid). Why can a single monomer form this polyester?
options: Each molecule has a C=C double bond, so it undergoes addition polymerisation without losing water
The OH group reacts with another OH group, forming ester links that release hydrogen gas
The COOH group reacts with another COOH group, forming ester links that release carbon dioxide
Each molecule has both an OH group and a COOH group, so it can form ester links at both ends
questions.explanation: An ester forms between an OH and a COOH. A hydroxy acid carries one of each, so molecules can join head to tail by condensation, releasing water. The monomer has no C=C, so addition polymerisation is not possible.

questions.stem: A polyester fabric is soaked in hot sodium hydroxide solution and breaks down. What type of reaction occurs?
options: Oxidation of the ester links, forming carbon dioxide and water in solution
Neutralisation of the polymer's amino groups, forming a soluble ammonium salt
Alkaline hydrolysis of the ester links, forming a carboxylate salt and a diol
Addition of hydroxide across C=C bonds, forming a saturated diol and an acid
questions.explanation: Hydroxide hydrolyses ester links, so the chain breaks into the diol and the dicarboxylate salt. Polyesters have no C=C bonds or amino groups.

questions.stem: A section of a polyester is -OCH₂CH₂OCOCH₂CH₂CO-OCH₂CH₂OCOCH₂CH₂CO-. What are the products of its complete acidic hydrolysis?
questions.explanation: Breaking each ester link adds OH to the C=O carbon and H to the oxygen, giving ethane-1,2-diol and butanedioic acid. The dicarboxylate ion would form only under alkaline conditions.

questions.stem: Which functional group is formed when a carboxylic acid reacts with a primary amine?
questions.explanation: The COOH and NH₂ groups condense, losing water, to form an amide link. In proteins the same link is called a peptide link.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid reacts with methanamine in a condensation reaction. What is the amide product?
questions.explanation: The OH from the acid and an H from the amine's NH₂ are lost as water, joining CH₃CO- to -NHCH₃. The salt CH₃COO⁻ CH₃NH₃⁺ forms when the two simply undergo proton transfer without condensation.

questions.stem: The amide CH₃CH₂CONHCH₂CH₃ was made by condensation. Which pair of reactants was used?
questions.explanation: The part bonded to the C=O, CH₃CH₂CO-, comes from propanoic acid; the part on the nitrogen, -NHCH₂CH₃, comes from ethanamine. Ethanol would give an ester, not an amide.

questions.stem: Which pair of monomers is used to make nylon-6,6?
questions.explanation: Nylon-6,6 is a polyamide: each monomer has two functional groups, and each has six carbons. Monomers with one group each give only a single amide, and a diol with a diacid gives a polyester.

questions.stem: What is the repeating unit of nylon-6,6?
questions.explanation: Hexane-1,6-diamine contributes -NH(CH₂)₆NH-, and hexanedioic acid contributes -CO(CH₂)₄CO-, since two of its six carbons are C=O carbons. The O version is a polyester.

questions.stem: An amide is heated with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which products form?
options: An ester and ammonia gas, which bubbles out of solution
A carboxylic acid and the protonated amine (an ammonium salt)
A carboxylate salt and the neutral amine molecule
An alcohol and an amine, with no other product
questions.explanation: Acidic hydrolysis breaks the C-N bond. The amine released is a base, so in the acid it is protonated to an ammonium ion, while the acid part stays as the carboxylic acid.

questions.stem: N-methylethanamide, CH₃CONHCH₃, is heated with sodium hydroxide solution. What are the products?
questions.explanation: In alkaline hydrolysis the acid part is deprotonated to ethanoate, and the amine is released as the neutral molecule, CH₃NH₂. Ethanoic acid with methylammonium ions is the result of acidic hydrolysis.

questions.stem: Paracetamol contains an amide link between an ethanoyl group, CH₃CO-, and 4-aminophenol. It is heated with dilute acid. What forms?
options: Ethanol and 4-aminophenol with its amino group oxidised
Ethanoic acid and phenol, with ammonia gas released
Ethanoic acid and the protonated form of 4-aminophenol
Ethanoate ions and the neutral 4-aminophenol molecule
questions.explanation: Acidic hydrolysis of the amide link gives the carboxylic acid, ethanoic acid, and the amine, 4-aminophenol, which is protonated by the excess acid. Ethanoate ions would form in alkaline conditions.

questions.stem: Kevlar is a polyamide used in protective vests. Why does it slowly lose strength when kept in hot, humid conditions for long periods?
options: Its amide links are slowly hydrolysed by water, breaking the polymer chains
Water adds across its C=C double bonds, converting the chains into alcohols
Water dissolves the ionic bonds that hold the polymer chains together
Heat converts its amide links into ester links, which are much weaker
questions.explanation: Amide links can be hydrolysed, and warmth and moisture over time speed this up, shortening the chains. The chains are held to each other by hydrogen bonds, not ionic bonds.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the formation of polyesters and polyamides?
options: Polyesters form by addition and polyamides by condensation polymerisation
Both form by hydrolysis of their monomers in acidic or alkaline solution
Both form by condensation polymerisation, releasing a small molecule such as water
Both form by addition polymerisation of monomers containing C=C double bonds
questions.explanation: Ester and amide links both form by condensation, with water released at each link. Addition polymerisation needs C=C bonds and releases no small molecule; hydrolysis is the reverse process that breaks these links.
